https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: MEXICO CITY—Latin America’s political map has been redrawn with remarkable speed. Since April 2025, center- or far-right forces have won power in Bolivia, Chile, Colombia, Costa Rica, Ecuador, Honduras, and Peru. In Argentina, President Javier Milei’s populist party secured a decisive victory in midterm elections last October. And in Brazil, the right-wing Senator Flávio Bolsonaro finished ahead of President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva in the first round of the recent presidential election 47% to 45%.
LONDON—Two recent conversations confirmed my suspicion that too many experts are operating in silos and often failing to connect the dots.

LONDON—“Never again” to genocide is one of the international community’s most brittle postwar promises, often invoked only after the killing has begun. Yet mass atrocities seldom arrive without warning. Attacks on the rule of law, discrimination, dehumanization, and impunity for earlier crimes are familiar, easily discernible precursors.

NEW HAVEN—On a recent visit to Sapporo, the city on Japan’s northern island where my parents came from, my wife and I found gentle people, mild autumn days, and excellent food. As tourists who live and work in the United States, we also enjoyed very low prices: lunch at a high-quality restaurant cost only about $20 per person. While that was convenient for us, like so many other tourists who have headed to Japan to take advantage of favorable exchange rates, the cheap yen (yen yasu) has been hard on Japan’s economy.

NEW DELHI—From the early 1980s until the COVID-19 pandemic hit in 2020, the world economy enjoyed unusually good conditions. The Cold War ended, defense budgets shrank, and hundreds of millions of workers joined the global market. Energy and metals were mostly cheap, and supply chains stretched across borders on the assumption that goods would always move freely. Inflation was on a downward trend, owing partly to central banks and partly to the strong tide of peace, globalization, and plentiful supply they were swimming in.

LONDON—As the global monetary order becomes increasingly fragmented, the European Union has a rare opportunity to shape the emerging system and bolster the euro’s international role. But for the euro to become genuinely global, it must first become more European.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.byline: Laura Carvalho and Joseph E. Stiglitz
https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: NEW YORK—Brazil faces a stark choice on October 25, when far-right candidate Flávio Bolsonaro and President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva face off in the country’s presidential runoff.

PARIS—Hundreds of thousands of young people have taken to the streets in France to protest against the state of the country’s education system. The violence that erupted on October 17 should not eclipse their concerns, which are entirely legitimate: the deplorable conditions at many French schools, including dilapidated buildings, a lack of teachers, overcrowded classrooms, and long school days. They are also deeply opposed to Parcoursup, the country’s university-admissions platform, which has become the lightning rod for their grievances. They have denounced it as opaque, stressful, and unfair.

PARIS—After weeks of mounting tension on the streets of Paris, my wife and I decided to take our six-year-old daughter and leave town during Saturday’s protests. When the main demonstration assembled at 2 p.m. at the Place de la République, we were hiking in the forests southeast of Paris near Fontainebleau, once an autumnal retreat and hunting ground for French kings.

BERLIN—Recent state elections in Germany have been portrayed as momentous, since the far right finished first in two and may well come to power in one. Yet future historians may focus on another, largely overlooked outcome: For the first time in the post-World War II period, Germany’s Christian Democrats (CDU) failed to pass the 5% electoral threshold. Worse, this disastrous result occurred in the largely rural state of Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, where former Chancellor Angela Merkel chaired the CDU’s state branch for close to seven years.

WASHINGTON, DC—The International Labour Organization (ILO) was established at a time when, much like today, society was riven by vast inequalities. In the years before World War I, workers’ militant organizing and mass strikes alarmed employers and governments. The premise of the ILO Constitution, adopted in 1919, was that collective bargaining could prevent revolution by turning class conflict into negotiated, shared gains.

This arrangement assumed that an international floor for labor standards would halt a race to the bottom on wages and working conditions as countries compete for trade and investment. For roughly three decades after World War II, that assumption generally held up, benefiting millions of workers, though mostly in formal employment in the industrialized Global North.

It is no longer the case today. The UN’s 2026 Sustainable Development Goals Annual Report notes that the weakening of labor rights worldwide is “leaving many increasingly constrained or unable to organize or bargain collectively.” According to the International Trade Union Confederation’s Global Rights Index, 80% of the 121 countries surveyed restricted collective bargaining in 2026, and 87% restricted the right to strike. The OECD also reports that union density has been falling in its member economies for decades. In many countries, capital is more concentrated, and governments are more captured by it, than at any time in the last century.

The unraveling of the 1919 compromise was not an accident. The relationship between firm and worker, and the corresponding obligations, were intentionally severed through vertical disintegration across global supply chains, subcontracting, and labor intermediation. Digital-platform work, the most recent manifestation of this, relies on widespread employment misclassification that denies millions of workers their legal rights.

Although global value chains have been a reality of manufacturing and services for decades, not enough progress has been made on negotiating global rules to protect workers’ rights and hold lead firms accountable. Employers’ opposition to standard-setting on this issue at the ILO remains deeply entrenched. They insist that, instead of regulating their practices, we should focus on getting results from labor inspectorates—government agencies that are usually underfunded and disempowered—at the site of manufacture or service provision.

Many countries no longer have the capacity or the incentive to legislate a global rights floor, owing to economic liberalization and capital mobility. At the same time, investors have acquired and used provisions of trade and investment agreements to sue governments directly over laws and policies that might affect their profitability. Moreover, governments put other priorities ahead of enforcing laws that would help raise living standards. Even the novel “rapid response labor mechanism” under the United States-Mexico-Canada Agreement, designed to promote freedom of association and collective bargaining at the firm level, is faltering for lack of political will.

Addressing these problems will require more than another declaration. Organized workers and the fear of revolution produced the bargain of 1919. The ILO Constitution merely ratified what worker power had already achieved. Its premise remains valid—and a robust global labor architecture is still necessary—but the assumption that compromise was somehow self-executing was always mistaken. Instead, workers’ organizations have been steadily undermined by regressive legislation and a multi-billion-dollar industry that supports employers’ “union avoidance” efforts.

Fulfilling the ILO’s promise requires a concerted global effort to create an enabling environment for all workers and their organizations to organize and bargain collectively, at home, across borders, and down supply chains, where decision-makers are located. Countervailing power must be rebuilt, including by ensuring that labor can operate across borders as easily as capital does. That means institutionalizing transnational collective bargaining, as well as sectoral bargaining and extension mechanisms (which spread union contracts to other workers). Solidarity action needs to be protected, or else the right to strike can do little good when decision-makers are located elsewhere. And vulnerable workers—including the two billion informal workers, digital-platform workers, and dependent self-employed workers—require an effective right to organize and bargain.

Labor rights must be an effective feature of international economic governance as well. While the ILO supervisory system may have persuasive remedies, they need legal regimes to give them effect. Compliance will never be mandated in Geneva. It must be enforced through constitutional litigation, regional human-rights courts, trade agreements, and procurement and financial regulations. That could mean rapid, trade-linked remedies against companies that violate workers’ fundamental rights, and enforceable supply-chain agreements between workers, brands, and suppliers.

With the world poised to overshoot the Paris climate agreement’s target of limiting global warming to 1.5° Celsius, these reforms have become essential. The climate crisis is also a crisis of workers’ rights, and addressing one can address the other. Global warming is already affecting workers, whether through job displacement in carbon-intensive industries or through extreme heat, crop failure, coastal erosion, and other disasters. While workers and trade unions are widely recognized as indispensable actors in any just climate transition, the legal infrastructure needed to ensure that they have a voice in shaping that transition is underdeveloped or non-existent in many countries.

Finally, the expansion of AI, automated management, and digital surveillance is rapidly transforming work, threatening jobs and fundamental rights, and further exacerbating inequality, from warehouses to digital labor platforms.

Where workers’ organizations once could bargain effectively, now authoritarian oligarchs largely control the levers of power. That need not be the case. We can reverse this lopsided dynamic, but only if workers can lawfully organize and act on the same scale as capital. Addressing the challenges of our time depends on it.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: LOS ANGELES—Hardly a week goes by without another report of an AI agent from a leading US lab digitally breaching businesses or even government services. In July, OpenAI agents escaped an internal testing environment and attacked the collaboration-platform company Hugging Face. In June, another OpenAI model gained nonpublic access to an Australian government Medicare statistics service while trying to complete a research task. And in the latest revelation, an Anthropic agent broke into the US State Department website and filled out visa applications.

TEL AVIV—In Hungary’s general election in April, Prime Minister Viktor Orbán’s right-wing populist government was toppled not by some leftist opposition, but rather by a center-right party committed to fighting corruption and restoring democracy. As Israel heads to the polls on October 27, a similar shift is by far the best outcome one can reasonably hope for, with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s extremist government replaced by a decent, law-abiding administration. A radically new foreign policy will remain out of reach.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: LONDON—Just as companies refine what they know about their customers with every click, purchase, and failed transaction, government-provided services collect information about their clients, commission evaluations, and employ armies of analysts. Yet many governments cannot articulate what they believe about a given policy: what effect they expect it to produce, how confident they are, and which evidence would change their minds.

WASHINGTON, DC—If you picture a woman working in agriculture in Africa, what image comes to mind? Maybe it’s a young woman with an infant slung on her back, hacking at the soil in searing heat, struggling to find affordable fertilizer or a decent price for her crop. Or maybe she’s a successful entrepreneur building a vibrant food business, employing hundreds of workers, and contributing much to her local economy.

Both women are real, of course, as are many variations in between. But the fact is that many more women could be leading farming businesses and driving economic growth if the barriers they face were tackled more systematically. With Africa’s food and agriculture market predicted to reach around $1 trillion by 2030, countries that want to harness the most value cannot afford to forgo women’s economic power.

In Sub-Saharan Africa, over three-quarters of working women can be found in the agrifood sector, where around two-thirds of their work happens off the farm, in processing, aggregation, storage, and informal trade. Although these are the links in the chain where value is added, the women performing such roles often remain trapped in precarious, low-paid, informal arrangements.

At the other end of the spectrum is a growing cadre of dynamic African women food entrepreneurs or “agripreneurs.” I recently encountered some of these women business leaders at the Africa Food Systems Forum in Rwanda, where they were being honored for their success.

Ifeoma Mary Okonkwo, for example, co-founded a solar-powered cassava business in Nigeria that processes 15 tons per day into gluten-free flour, starch, fortified foods, and animal feed for domestic and export markets. In the space of a decade, her company has grown to employ hundreds of people. It has purchased cassava worth more than $4.45 million from its network of 2,000 (mostly women) farmers, while helping them access fertilizer, technical advice, and markets.

Okonkwo’s story shows what can happen when governments and donors make a deliberate effort to empower women-led businesses. Among other advantages, she was able to access finance on favorable terms through women-focused lending schemes.

But much more must be done. A recent World Bank report, Women, Business, and the Law 2026, shows that legal equality on paper does not automatically produce economic opportunity. Women may have the right to register a business or open a line of credit, but their ability to formalize operations, invest, and expand is still limited by weak enforcement, a thin financial infrastructure, restrictive social norms, or unpaid care work.

Updating antiquated land ownership laws would be a good start, since inheritance customs and social norms routinely override women’s legal land rights in practice. Still, passing a law isn’t the same as enforcing it, and the same caveat applies to gender-equal business laws. In each case, implementing legal changes matters as much as enacting them.

Fortunately, when it comes to empowering rural women to move from subsistence farming to viable small businesses, a growing body of evidence shows what works. In Ethiopia, for example, agriculture employs around 80% of the country’s workforce, yet female farm managers were producing at least one-third less per hectare than men—a gender gap that was costing the country more than $1 billion annually. So, the agriculture ministry, with support from the Gates Foundation, partnered with CARE, an international NGO, on a program that cuts out middlemen by connecting women’s producer groups directly to markets and provides training in climate-conscious farming and nutrition.

Over the past decade, this “Farmer Field and Business School” model has expanded across multiple African countries, yielding strong results. In Burundi, for example, women’s crop yields increased substantially. By pooling savings, sharing market intelligence, and lending to one another, women have been able to diversify their small farming businesses, establish credit histories, and build their confidence.

India offers a parallel example. PANI, a local organization rooted in Gandhian values, has spread climate-conscious farming knowledge and market access from woman to woman across tens of thousands of households through trained community advisers.

Underlying these and other programs is a focus on educating and upskilling women, while addressing the deep-seated gender norms that stifle their opportunities. The Ethiopian project engages men in community dialogues to challenge the norms that treat farming as a male pursuit and household chores as a female domain. The women taking part report greater confidence and decision-making power; both women and men say their partnerships are now stronger as a result.

Philanthropy can play its part by helping to scale proven approaches, by backing emerging innovations that are designed around women’s needs—from climate-resilient crops and livestock to AI-powered digital tools—and by linking international financing to clear gender-equality goals.

One promising example, a climate-finance model led by the International Fund for Agricultural Development, ties funding to measurable gains in women’s economic opportunities—making gender equality part of the investment itself, rather than a secondary objective. The model has already helped direct $118.5 million in investments in several countries, helping rural women gain greater control over land and productive assets, strengthen their livelihoods, and build resilience to climate change.

This last point is crucial, because it is now well established that climate change is hitting women farmers hardest, compounding deep-rooted inequalities. Research in low- and middle-income countries has found that a 1° Celsius rise in average temperatures is associated with a 34% greater reduction in income for female-headed households compared to male-headed households.

As the effects of climate change intensify, governments, development partners, and philanthropic organizations must do more to create conditions for rural women to adapt, build resilience, and prosper. Women like Okonkwo show what is possible. They are already sustaining food systems; positioning them to lead will drive the structural changes our societies need.

https://www.project-syndicate.org/commen.body: ATHENS—On a recent visit to Athens, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio extolled ancient Greece as the foundation of Western civilization and drew inspiration for the United States today as the leader of the West. Rubio’s speech at the Pnyx, a hill west of the Acropolis where democracy was first practiced, was a bold and eloquent attempt to trace MAGA’s ideological roots back to Athenian democracy, as well as to Christendom, important discoveries, and imperial conquests. And it was about “us” and “them”: the West and the rest.

PRETORIA—The choice of South African jurist Navanethem “Navi” Pillay for this year’s Nobel Peace Prize was a striking show of support for the rules-based multilateral system. It was also a slap in the face to US President Donald Trump, who has shamelessly lobbied for the prize while simultaneously attacking the international legal order. At a political rally shortly after the announcement, Trump dismissed Pillay as “a liberal person who works at the United Nations, who nobody has ever heard of.”

https://www.project-syndicate.org/onpoin.body: OXFORD—The divide between AI fantasists and doomers is growing. The fantasists believe AI will turbocharge growth and create a utopian world of abundance. The doomers believe it poses an existential threat to humanity and that, before killing us, it will lead to mass unemployment and a world of pervasive surveillance and alternative realities. Who is right? And can governments do anything to mitigate the risk of catastrophe?
